generalfeedback.text:
For a statement ‘if A, then B’: a direct proof assumes A and aims for B; a proof of the contrapositive assumes not B and aims for not A; a proof by contradiction assumes A and not B and aims for something impossible. All three prove the statement. A proof that assumes B and aims for A proves the converse; one that assumes not A and aims for not B proves a different statement again (it is the contrapositive of the converse). Neither proves the statement, even when the converse happens to be true as well.

The five lines for this statement:

  • {@ldir@} This starts a direct proof.

  • {@lcp@} This starts a proof of the contrapositive.

  • {@lcon@} This starts a proof by contradiction.

  • {@lconv@} This starts a proof of the converse, a different statement.

  • {@linv@} This starts a proof of ‘if not A, then not B’, a different statement.

{@best@}

H. S., Roberts, S. and Downey, F., Thinking about Proof, 1st edition, University of Southampton, 2022.
